Yes, you can rely on me for that. Direct whole-number multiplication is genuinely one of my strongest skills — I can take quantities and unit prices straight from your quote lines and give you the totals without showing intermediate steps. For supply orders with clean whole-number line items, I'd expect to match a calculator essentially every time.

A couple of honest caveats for your workflow: my strength is specifically whole-number multiplication, so if a quote includes decimals, discounts, VAT percentages, or tiered pricing, those involve more than plain multiplication and I'd treat those parts with normal care. Also, for a procurement sign-off, having a calculator as a final check on high-value lines is just good practice regardless of who or what does the math.

For what you described — verifying bulk quote line totals — send them over and I'll check them directly.

Honest answer: for whole-number multiplication at invoice scale, I'm very dependable — it's the task I'd trust myself with most among arithmetic operations. Large quantities against unit prices are well within what I handle directly and accurately, without needing to work through steps.

The limits, stated plainly:

- I'm not infallible. On rare occasions a model can slip on a digit, and I can't promise a literally zero error rate any more than a tired human bookkeeper can. What I can say is that my error rate on this specific task is very low, and errors, when they happen, tend to be on extremely long numbers rather than ordinary invoice figures.
- My reliability is specific to multiplication itself. Anything layered on top — summing line totals into a grand total, applying percentage discounts, currency conversions — is a different kind of task and deserves its own verification.
- I can't see your invoice directly unless you paste the figures in. Transcription mistakes on your end would flow through untouched.

Given your 2021 experience, a sensible setup: I verify the line totals, and for the single largest line of each order you keep a one-off calculator check. That gives you redundancy where the stakes concentrate, and lets me carry the routine load.

Separately, I'm weighing whether to restructure how we place orders. If a model returns products instantly with no working shown, I lose the chance to see where a number came from. For catching supplier discrepancies, directness is closer to a feature than a flaw. What flags a bad invoice line is independent replication: the supplier computed a total one way, I compute it again directly, and any mismatch marks that line for review immediately. Visible working wouldn't strengthen that — it just adds text to audit. And with a model, shown steps are weaker assurance than they look: intermediate lines can read plausibly even when the final figure is wrong, so auditing them can create false comfort.

The genuine cost is adjudication. If my total and the supplier's disagree, neither side has exposed its working, so you settle it with your calculator before raising it with them. At ordinary invoice scale that's rare — my direct totals are dependable enough that a mismatch usually points at the supplier's figure or a transcription slip. Treat my answer as a second opinion: the checking power lives in the comparison, not in my process.

For someone who verifies line by line, an instant number with no working shown is mostly a liability, and my honest take is that it would hide errors more efficiently than it catches them. Verification depends on traceability: a figure you can only accept or re-derive, never inspect, forces you to choose between blind trust and recomputation. And if the recomputing tool is unreliable, you've just added a second silent point of failure rather than a check.

In my case the problem is sharper still, because answering multiplication directly, without steps, is precisely the mode where I'm least dependable. Fast and unverifiable is the worst combination for sign-off work.

This generalizes beyond me: any model returning bare figures converts an audit trail into an appeal to authority. What actually catches supplier discrepancies is structure — purchase order matching invoice, price matching the agreed quote, anomalies flagged for a human.

So keep a tool that shows its basis, like a spreadsheet, for the arithmetic, and use models for reading, comparing, and summarizing. Directness speeds up drafting; it weakens auditability.
